newsitem.title: Russia: Yeltsin plans rare trip abroad for Clinton summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin plans rare trip abroad for Clinton summit.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin, grounded in Russia since June with health problems, will travel to Helsinki next month for a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton, officials said on Friday.

The Helskini summit, announced by U.S. Vice President Al Gore, was relocated from the United States to reduce the strain on the Kremlin leader, who underwent heart surgery in November and then developed pneumonia last month.
"This of course will be an important meeting," Gore told a joint news conference with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in Washington.

"We expect among other things that the presidents will address bilateral arms control, European security and a number of economic issues of importance to our peoples," Gore said after announcing that the summit would held on March 20 and 21.

Yeltsin, the vigour and colour of earlier days clearly faded, remained secluded at his country home on Friday while his defence chiefs made a joint public appearance in Moscow designed to show the hand of presidential control.

The 66-year-old president, who had quintuple bypass heart surgery on November 5 and developed pneumonia on January 6, is clearly eager to show he controls defence and foreign policy during diplomatic exchanges with the West over NATO's expansion plans.

He has been on a "working convalescence" outside Moscow almost continuously since he was reelected in July. Earlier this month he cancelled a trip to The Hague to meet the acting president of the European Union on the advice of his doctors.

It had been the U.S. turn to host the summit, but officials said it had been moved to Helsinki in deference to the health problems suffered by Yeltsin, whose last foreign trip was to neighbouring Belarus in June.
Finland borders Russia, meaning that the Russian president could travel by land or take a one-hour flight.

NATO will be high on the agenda at the Clinton-Yeltsin summit and Yeltsin must be seen to extract some kind of formal acknowledgement of Russian concerns before the alliance issues invitations to ex-Warsaw Pact states at a Madrid summit in July.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Friday reasserted Moscow's objections to the alliance expansion and added the latest in a series of warnings.

"If Russia's concerns are not taken into account, under these conditions we would be forced to think of very serious changes, including in the conduct of foreign relations," Primakov told journalists, without elaborating.
Yeltsin met his chief aide Anatoly Chubais for 40 minutes on Friday while his defence chiefs made a joint public appearance to dispel reports of squabbling over reform.

"Rumours about what they describe as our rivalry are unfounded," Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said of his relations with Kremlin Defence Council secretary Yuri Baturin. "We may express different views. But it is the commander-in-chief (Yeltsin) who issues final orders which we have to obey."

The event showed Yeltsin, despite his physical absence from the Kremlin for all but a few hours in recent weeks, publicly imposing his will on defence chiefs. Rodionov, however, offered little cheer to his superior.
Asked about Yeltsin's absences from work, he replied: "I would really like to see our commander-in-chief back, healthy and capable of working as he has done in the past.
"Now I have to wait for better times. One is left to hope that contacts which existed between commander-in-chief and defence minister will soon be restored."
Rodionov said on Thursday night that the armed forces had decayed to a "horrifying state". He said if reforms were delayed, nuclear systems could be out of control in two years.
